<!-- Generated from guide-unity.html by scripts/build-agent-docs.js. Do not edit by hand. -->
Source: https://manticorp.github.io/unrealheightmap/guide-unity.html
Title: Unity Guide · 16/32 Bit Heightmap Generator
Summary: Import real-world heightmaps into Unity Terrain at true scale: converting to 16-bit RAW, terrain sizing, splatmaps from height bands, and GLB meshes with glTFast.

# Unity: Terrain import at real-world scale

This works the same in Unity 2022 LTS and Unity 6. Unity's Terrain imports 16-bit RAW heightmaps with sides of 2n+1 pixels, so the work is mostly choosing the right export and converting it.

## 1\. Export

-   **Format:** PNG 16-bit.
-   **Size:** a square 2n+1. Type **1025**, **2049** or **4097** into Output Width and Height. The largest Unity Terrain heightmap is 4097. For more, use a tiled export with 2049 or 4097 tiles and one Terrain per tile.
-   **Normalisation:** Smart.
-   **Extra Outputs:** OpenGL normal map and height bands, if you want them.

Note the **height range** (lowest and highest in metres) and the area width in metres.

## 2\. Convert to RAW

Unity's Import Raw reads headerless 16-bit grayscale, little-endian ("Windows" byte order). With [ImageMagick](https://imagemagick.org) 7:

```
magick heightmap.png -depth 16 -endian LSB gray:heightmap.raw
```

If your export isn't already 2n+1 (for example 1024 or 2048), pad it by repeating the edge pixels:

```
magick heightmap.png -virtual-pixel edge -set option:distort:viewport 1025x1025+0+0 -filter point -distort SRT 0 -depth 16 -endian LSB gray:heightmap.raw
```

On ImageMagick 6, use `convert`. In Photoshop, save as **Photoshop Raw** with **IBM PC** byte order, keeping the image in 16 Bits/Channel mode.

## 3\. Import into a Terrain

1.  **GameObject → 3D Object → Terrain.**
2.  Select it, open **Terrain Settings** (gear icon) → **Texture Resolutions (On Terrain Data)** → **Import Raw…**, and pick the `.raw` file.
3.  In the Import Heightmap window:
    -   **Depth**: Bit 16
    -   **Resolution**: detected from the file size. Check it reads 1025, 2049 or 4097.
    -   **Byte Order**: Windows
    -   **Terrain Size**: X = Z = the area width in metres, and Y = the **height range** in metres
    -   **Flip Vertically**: Unity puts the first image row (north) at the terrain's −Z edge. Tick it if you want north at +Z.
4.  Set the Terrain's Transform **Position Y** to the **lowest height** for absolute heights.

**Example:** a 2049 px export covering 13.5 km, with heights from 120 m to 1,620 m.

Terrain Size `13500, 1500, 13500`, Position Y `120`.

-   **Height limit:** Terrain Height must be between 1 and 10,000 m, which fits every real-world range.
-   **Unpadded size:** Width and Length = (pixels − 1) × metres per pixel. If you padded a 1024 export to 1025, the extra pixel adds one metres-per-pixel step of width.

### Terrain Toolbox alternative

The **Terrain Tools** package (`com.unity.terrain-tools`) adds **Window → Terrain → Terrain Toolbox**. Its Create New Terrain → **Import Heightmap** can build several tiled terrains from a batch of RAW files, and has **Height Remap** and **Flip Axis** options. Use RAW files there too. 16-bit PNGs imported as Unity textures may lose precision.

## 4\. Terrain layers from the height bands

Unity stores terrain painting in splatmaps: RGBA textures where each channel is one Terrain Layer. Layer 1 is red, layer 2 green, layer 3 blue and layer 4 alpha, and the next splatmap carries on with layer 5. The tool's height bands add up to white, so they make a valid splatmap.

1.  Pack up to four band masks into one RGBA image:
    
    ```
    magick *_band_00_*.png *_band_01_*.png *_band_02_*.png *_band_03_*.png -set colorspace sRGB -combine -define png:color-type=6 splat0.png
    ```
    
    If you padded the heightmap, pad the bands to the terrain's **Control Texture Resolution** too (or resize them to it).
2.  Create Terrain Layers (grass, rock, snow and so on) on the Terrain, in the same order as the bands.
3.  Apply the image with Terrain Toolbox → **Terrain Utilities → Import Splatmaps** → add `splat0.png` → **Apply to Terrain**.

The OpenGL normal map and albedo are whole-terrain textures. Unity's Terrain Layers are tiling textures, so use them in a custom terrain shader, or on a mesh exported from the tool (below).

## 5\. Meshes instead of Terrain

-   **GLB:** install **glTFast** (Package Manager → **+** → Install package by name → `com.unity.cloud.gltfast`). Version 6.18 is the last that supports 2022.3; newer versions need Unity 6. GLB files then import like any model, at 1 unit = 1 m.
-   **OBJ:** imports natively. Check the **Scale Factor** and tick **Generate Colliders** on the Model tab.
-   Export with **Top surface only** and **Real world (metres)**. The UVs cover the top, so the albedo and OpenGL normal map line up in a standard Lit material.

## Troubleshooting

The Import Raw resolution is wrong, or the terrain is noise

The file isn't 16-bit little-endian, or isn't a square 2n+1. Re-run the ImageMagick command with `-endian LSB`, check the file is exactly width × height × 2 bytes, and set Byte Order to Windows.

The terrain is terraced

The heightmap went through 8 bits somewhere. Convert from the tool's 16-bit PNG directly, and choose Depth: Bit 16 in the import window.

The mountains are the wrong height

Terrain Size Y must equal the height range of _that_ export. Unity maps white to the full Terrain Height.

Tiled terrains don't line up in height

All tiles from one tiled export share one height scale, so give every Terrain the same Size Y and Position Y. For separate exports, set the same Norm From and Norm To in the tool.

## References

-   [Unity manual: working with heightmaps](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/terrain-Heightmaps.html)
-   [Terrain Toolbox: Import Heightmap](https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.terrain-tools@5.3/manual/toolbox-import-heightmap.html) and [Import Splatmaps](https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.terrain-tools@5.3/manual/toolbox-import-splatmaps.html)
-   [glTFast installation](https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.cloud.gltfast@6.20/manual/installation.html)

<!-- Generated from guide-3d-printing.html by scripts/build-agent-docs.js. Do not edit by hand. -->
Source: https://manticorp.github.io/unrealheightmap/guide-3d-printing.html
Title: 3D Printing Guide · 16/32 Bit Heightmap Generator
Summary: Print real-world terrain: choosing area, size, height exaggeration and base thickness, then slicing in PrusaSlicer, Bambu Studio or Cura.

# 3D printing real terrain

The tool exports a watertight, ready-to-slice STL, so you don't need any other software.

## 1\. Choose the area

-   **Frame your area with some relief.** A mountain, a valley or a volcano. Flat farmland prints as a flat slab.
-   **Output zoom.** The STL uses the area shown by the orange rectangle. Very high zooms don't add printable detail: on a 150 mm print, a 0.4 mm nozzle resolves about 375 points across. For a 20 km area, zoom 12 to 13 data is plenty, and Mapterhorn lidar areas give the crispest small prints.
-   Check it in **3D Preview** first, with the exaggeration you plan to use.

## 2\. Export settings

3D Model Format

**STL**

Mesh Resolution

**512** for prints up to about 150 mm. **1024** for larger prints or very rugged terrain. Beyond that, files grow large with no visible gain at nozzle scale.

Shape

**Solid with base**. This makes a closed, flat-bottomed model that needs no supports.

Base Thickness

**2 to 3 mm** under the lowest point. Use more for large prints to prevent warping, or if you want to engrave a label on the side.

Scale

**Print size (mm)**, with Print Width set to the length of the longer side.

Height Exaggeration

**1** for alpine terrain. **1.5 to 2** for hills. **2 to 3** for gentle landscapes, coasts and plains. Real terrain looks surprisingly flat at small scale: at 150 mm wide, a 20 km area with 1,500 m of relief is only 11 mm tall at 1×.

After generating a heightmap, the output also shows the height/width ratio, and how tall the print would be at 100 mm wide with no exaggeration.

## 3\. Slicing

STL files have no units. The tool writes millimetres, which every slicer assumes.

-   **Check the size** shown in the slicer matches your Print Width. In PrusaSlicer, decline the "convert from inches" prompt, which only applies to genuine inch files.
-   **Orientation:** flat on the base. No supports are needed.
-   **Layer height:** 0.08 to 0.12 mm shows contours best. Variable layer height saves time by using thin layers only near the peaks:
    -   PrusaSlicer: select the model → **Variable layer height** → **Adaptive**.
    -   Bambu Studio: **Variable layer height** (adaptive).
    -   Cura: **Experimental → Use Adaptive Layers**.
-   **Walls and infill:** 2 to 3 walls and 10 to 15% infill. Use 4 or more top layers so the terrain surface is solid.
-   **Seam:** place it at the back or on a sharp corner, so it doesn't run down a mountainside.
-   **Ironing:** leave it off. It flattens the contours you want to see.

These are typical settings that work well for terrain. Adjust them for your printer and material.

## 4\. Make it look great

-   **Colour by height:** on single-nozzle printers, add colour changes at layer heights, for example green, then grey at the treeline, then white for snow. Work out the layer height for a real altitude:
    
    ```
    print Z (mm) = base + (altitude − lowest) × exaggeration × print width ÷ area width (m) ÷ 1000
    ```
    
    Multi-material printers (AMS, MMU) can do the same with height-range modifiers.
-   **Water:** export with **Flatten below water level** so lakes and the sea print as perfectly flat surfaces. That's ideal for a colour change, or for pouring resin afterwards.
-   **Tiles:** for prints larger than your bed, export neighbouring areas at the same output zoom and the same Norm From / Norm To, so the heights match. Print them at the same Print Width and exaggeration.
-   **Resin printers:** use a thinner base (1.5 to 2 mm), hollow large models in your resin slicer, and add drain holes in the base.

## Troubleshooting

The print is tiny, or 25 times too big

The slicer converted units. Re-import and decline any inch conversion, or check the importer's unit setting. The STL is in millimetres.

Thin spikes or jagged ridges

Lower the Mesh Resolution or the exaggeration. Very sharp ridges narrower than your nozzle can't print cleanly.

The slicer says the mesh has errors

"Solid with base" models are built watertight. If a slicer still complains, run its repair function (it should find nothing to fix) and check you didn't export "Top surface only", which is an open skin.

Source: https://manticorp.github.io/unrealheightmap/guide-other.html
Title: QGIS, Gaea, World Machine & Houdini Guide · 16/32 Bit Heightmap Generator
Summary: Use real-world heightmaps in QGIS (georeferenced, rescaled to metres), Gaea, World Machine, Houdini, Photoshop and Substance Designer.

# GIS, terrain tools and image editors

All of these start from the **16-bit PNG** export with **Smart** normalisation. Note the **height range** (lowest and highest in metres) and the **metres per pixel** shown after generating.

-   [QGIS and GDAL](https://manticorp.github.io/unrealheightmap/guide-other.md#qgis)
-   [Gaea](https://manticorp.github.io/unrealheightmap/guide-other.md#gaea)
-   [World Machine](https://manticorp.github.io/unrealheightmap/guide-other.md#worldmachine)
-   [Houdini](https://manticorp.github.io/unrealheightmap/guide-other.md#houdini)
-   [Photoshop, GIMP and Substance Designer](https://manticorp.github.io/unrealheightmap/guide-other.md#editors)

## QGIS and GDAL

### Load it in the right place

1.  Keep the PNG together with its `.pgw` world file and `.prj`, all with the same base name. The tool links them under the output, and they're included in zips.
2.  Drag the PNG into QGIS. GDAL reads the world file automatically, so the image lands in the right place.
3.  QGIS may not pick up the projection from the `.prj` next to a PNG. If the layer shows an unknown CRS, set it: right-click the layer → **Layer CRS → Set Layer CRS** → **EPSG:3857**.

### Turn pixel values into metres

The PNG holds normalised values from 0 to 65535, not metres. Convert with **Raster → Raster Calculator**, replacing 120 and 1620 with your height range:

```
120 + "heightmap@1" / 65535 * (1620 - 120)
```

Save the result as a GeoTIFF (Float32). It now holds true elevations in metres.

### Reproject before measuring

EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator) stretches horizontal distances by 1/cos(latitude). Slope, hillshade and distance tools then give wrong answers. Reproject first with **Raster → Projections → Warp (Reproject)**:

-   Target CRS: your local UTM zone (for example EPSG:32632 for the Alps).
-   Resampling: **Bilinear** or **Cubic**.

Then **Raster → Analysis → Hillshade / Slope** work correctly with a Z factor of 1.

### Command line

```
# georeference and rescale to metres in one go (heights 120–1620 m)
gdal_translate -a_srs EPSG:3857 -ot Float32 -scale 0 65535 120 1620 heightmap.png heightmap_m.tif
# reproject to UTM 32N at 10 m pixels
gdalwarp -t_srs EPSG:32632 -tr 10 10 -r cubic heightmap_m.tif heightmap_utm.tif
```

## Gaea

Use Gaea to add erosion, snow and detail on top of real terrain, then export maps for your engine.

1.  Set the terrain's world **Scale** to the area width in metres, and its **Height** to the height range in metres.
2.  Add a **File** node and load the 16-bit PNG. Gaea stores heights from 0 to 1 internally and multiplies them by the terrain Height, so a normalised PNG maps directly to true relative heights.
3.  Keep the source unclamped. Gaea's docs suggest **Raw** scale for most files.
4.  Add erosion nodes. Because the scale is real, erosion and flow features come out at plausible sizes.
5.  Export at Unreal sizes (2017, 4033) for Unreal, and use the same Z scale maths as in the [Unreal guide](https://manticorp.github.io/unrealheightmap/guide-unreal.md#scale). The range is the Gaea terrain Height.

Gaea's docs also describe a _Match / Correct Heights_ recipe for terrains that need absolute altitudes. See the [Gaea documentation](https://docs.gaea.app).

## World Machine

1.  Add a **File Input** device and load the 16-bit PNG.
2.  Under elevation mapping, choose **Specify** and enter the lowest and highest heights in metres. _Full Range_ would stretch it to the whole world height instead.
3.  Under **World Placement**, set its size to the area's width and height in metres (**Set in Layout…**), so it matches your world extents.
4.  Build erosion and texture outputs as usual. For tiled builds into Unreal, use World Machine's own tiled output.

See the [File Input documentation](https://help.world-machine.com/topic/file-input-and-output/).

## Houdini

1.  Add a **HeightField File** SOP and load the PNG, with **Type** set to Height.
2.  **Size Method**: **Grid Spacing**, set to the metres per pixel.
3.  **Height Scale**: the height range in metres.
4.  For absolute altitudes, add a **HeightField Transform** or a Volume Wrangle (`@height += 120;`, using your lowest height).
5.  Load the extra masks into a second HeightField File with Type **Mask** to drive erosion, scattering or layer exports.

See the [HeightField File documentation](https://www.sidefx.com/docs/houdini/nodes/sop/heightfield_file.html).

## Photoshop, GIMP and Substance Designer

The rule for all of them: **never let the heightmap drop to 8 bits**. One 8-bit save cuts 65,536 levels to 256, and the terrain comes out terraced.

-   **Photoshop:** the PNG opens in **16 Bits/Channel** mode (check **Image → Mode**). Edit in 16-bit, and save with **Save As** (PNG or TIFF). Some _Export As_ and _Save for Web_ paths write 8-bit. Avoid sharpening and levels with clipping, which flatten peaks and valleys.
-   **GIMP:** check **Image → Precision** shows 16-bit, and choose a _linear_ precision so edits don't apply a gamma curve. Export the PNG with 16 bpc (on by default for 16-bit images).
-   **Substance 3D Designer:** set the bitmap's colour space to raw or linear (non-colour) and graph precision to 16-bit or higher. Bitmap painting only works on 8-bit images, so do painting on separate masks.
-   **Extra maps** (slope, curvature, bands, water) are 8-bit masks by design. They're fine to edit, paint and blur in any editor.

Title: Examples · 16/32 Bit Heightmap Generator
Summary: Things people have made with heightmaps from the 16/32 Bit Heightmap Generator, including real-terrain snowmobile maps for the game Sledders.

# Examples

Below are some things people have made with heightmaps from this tool.

## Sledders backcountry maps by DeNard420

Three of the four most downloaded maps for the snowmobile game [Sledders](https://mod.io/g/sledders) (built in Unity) were made by **DeNard420**, and all of them start from terrain made with this tool. Together they have been downloaded more than 400,000 times on mod.io.

The process: find a real place worth riding, export a DEM of it here, then work it up in tools like Gaea, adding rocks, trees, a labelled topo map, and props such as cabins and power lines. The tree maps come from Kris Tapio (Tapios\_BackCountry\_Builds), who traces the real tree lines from high-resolution satellite imagery, so the trees in the game sit almost exactly where they do in real life, with realistic density and tree lines.

-   [Whistler, British Columbia](https://mod.io/g/sledders/m/whistler): big chutes and peaks, trails, roads and rivers cleared
-   [Jackson Hole, Wyoming](https://mod.io/g/sledders/m/jackson-hole2): close to 1:1 on the lower peaks
-   [Aspen, Colorado](https://mod.io/g/sledders/m/aspen-snowmass): jump lines, named chutes and ski runs
-   [Mount Rainier, Washington](https://mod.io/g/sledders/m/mt-rainier): glaciers, crevasses and a detailed topo map

Title: Data Licences · 16/32 Bit Heightmap Generator
Summary: Licences, attribution and usage rights for the elevation data and map imagery used by the 16/32 Bit Heightmap Generator.

# Map License Information

## AWS Terrain Tiles (Mapzen) Elevation Data

When "AWS Terrain Tiles" is chosen as the elevation data (the default), heights come from the [Terrain Tiles dataset on the Registry of Open Data on AWS](https://registry.opendata.aws/terrain-tiles/). [Mapzen](https://www.mapzen.com/blog/elevation/) originally built it, and the tiles stayed available as open data after Mapzen shut down.

It is not 100% clear what the usage rights for the heightmaps are now. This was the ["rights" page that appeared on the Mapzen site.](https://www.mapzen.com/rights/#services-and-data-sources)

This was their [attribution guidance](https://github.com/tilezen/joerd/blob/master/docs/attribution.md), specifically.

If in doubt, the following snippet should be included on your project:

© [Mapzen](https://www.mapzen.com/rights), [OpenStreetMap](https://openstreetmap.org/copyright), and [others](https://www.mapzen.com/rights/#services-and-data-sources).

```
© <a href="https://www.mapzen.com/rights">Mapzen</a>,  <a href="https://openstreetmap.org/copyright">OpenStreetMap</a> , and <a href="https://www.mapzen.com/rights/#services-and-data-sources">others</a>.
```

## Mapterhorn Elevation Data

When "Mapterhorn" is chosen as the elevation data, heights come from [Mapterhorn](https://mapterhorn.com), an open-data project that combines Copernicus GLO-30 worldwide with high-resolution national datasets, including USGS 3DEP for the USA and lidar for the UK and much of Europe.

Each source has its own licence. The full list is on the [Mapterhorn attribution page](https://mapterhorn.com/attribution). If in doubt, include:

© [Mapterhorn](https://mapterhorn.com/attribution) and the open-data sources listed there.

## NOAA ETOPO 2022 (Land and Sea Floor)

When "NOAA ETOPO 2022" is chosen, heights come from NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information, served through their DEM mosaic service. NOAA data is in the public domain. Please credit:

NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (2022): ETOPO 2022 15 Arc-Second Global Relief Model. [doi:10.25921/fd45-gt74](https://doi.org/10.25921/fd45-gt74)

## Mars, Moon and Mercury Elevation Data

Mars heights come from the MGS MOLA global DEM (463 m), Moon heights from the LRO LOLA global DEM (118 m) and Mercury heights from the MESSENGER global DEM (665 m), all NASA mission data published by [USGS Astrogeology](https://astrogeology.usgs.gov) and in the public domain. The Gale crater model is the 1 m HiRISE stereo DEM mosaic made for the Mars Science Laboratory (Curiosity) mission by NASA, JPL, the University of Arizona and USGS, also in the public domain. Please credit the mission science team, NASA and USGS Astrogeology. The Mars and Moon base maps are from [OpenPlanetaryMap](https://www.openplanetary.org/opm), built from NASA, USGS and ESA data; the Mercury and Gale crater base maps are drawn in your browser from the elevation data.

The treemap uses [ESA WorldCover](https://esa-worldcover.org) 2021 tree cover (© ESA WorldCover project 2021 / Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2021) processed by the ESA WorldCover consortium, CC BY 4.0), read through [Microsoft's Planetary Computer](https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/dataset/esa-worldcover), and in Switzerland the vegetation height model of the Swiss National Forest Inventory (© BAFU / WSL / swisstopo, [Swiss open government data](https://www.geo.admin.ch/en/general-terms-of-use-fsdi)). Leaf types come from OpenStreetMap. Please credit them when you publish work made with the treemap.

## OpenStreetMap Layers

The OpenStreetMap layer masks are drawn from data © [OpenStreetMap contributors](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), available under the [Open Database License (ODbL)](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/), fetched through the [Overpass API](https://overpass-api.de). If you publish something made with them, credit "© OpenStreetMap contributors".

## Other Maps (Preview and Albedo)

Each preview map shows a link to its copyright information at the bottom of the map display.

Albedo images made with "Generate Albedo" come from the selected preview map, so they're covered by that provider's terms. Some of these don't allow commercial use, so check before shipping them in a product.

Most map providers can be found [on the leaflet providers page](https://leaflet-extras.github.io/leaflet-providers/preview/).

## Place Search

Place search uses [Photon](https://photon.komoot.io) by Komoot, which uses data © [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright) contributors.
